kicker: Hotrod Outdoor Alaska Fishing · the big update
title: A boat, a camera, Bigfoot, three new places and a secret
lede: Everything on your list is in the build: the game is now Hotrod Outdoor Alaska Fishing, with a fishing boat and outboard on a trailer, nine rods and five kinds of arrows, a wardrobe behind a T-shirt button, an arcade announcer (FISH ON!, IT THREW THE HOOK!, NEW SPECIES!), bites that follow the weather and the time, a full-screen map with the fish of every place you have been, a small map out of the way, a RUN button, bears that come only for the fish in your cooler, a camera and photo album, three new places (Steaming Springs, Mosquito Flats and Shipwreck Cove) with odd jobs, three new legends and a very shy Bigfoot, sharper mountains, a new Bear Falls, textures at twice the resolution, and light that follows the hour. And now a secret on the mountain, on no map: Gus's paraglider on a far summit that glints from the valley, a glide to a key on a ledge no path reaches, and his chest of gold behind Bear Falls. The audits found 98 problems; all are fixed and tested again. Estimated time left on the list: none. The next steps are at the top.

sections.title: Estimated time left, and the next steps
sections.html:
Estimated time left on this list: none. Everything you asked for is in the build at the link above, and so is the newest item, the secret on the mountain (its own section below). Each feature was tested in a browser engine and the whole round was audited: five code reviews and my own checks for the big update, and two more reviews for the secret. Every problem they found is fixed and checked again (the audit and the tests are further down). The reel, which you said works as intended, was left alone.

Two things remain, and both wait for you:

  • Playing it on your iPhone. The web build at the link has everything. The iPhone app in the Xcode project takes its copy of the game when it is built, so it needs building again in Xcode to get this round.
  • The App Store preparations, skipped as you asked until you say go: new App Store pictures for the 6.9-inch iPhone and the 13-inch iPad showing the new places, the boat and the camera (and none of the secret); the store text under the new name; and the publishing guide brought up to date. That is about one working session.

Next steps

  1. Your play test. Tell me what feels off on the phone. The likely candidates are the boat's steering, the timing bar's speed, the announcer's volume against the engine and the river, how often Bigfoot shows up (rare on purpose), and now the glide: whether the ledge is too hard or too easy to land on, and whether the climb to the summit is too long.
  2. The App Store round, when you say go.
  3. Ideas for a next round, if you want one:
    • More of Gus: a second secret that only the paraglider reaches, such as a hidden lake on a plateau with a fish found nowhere else.
    • A weekend fishing derby at the Trading Post, with a board of the heaviest fish of the weekend, in the spirit of Alaska's real fishing tournaments.
    • Winter: ice fishing on Glacier Lake with an auger and a shanty, snow on the roads and the hot rod on studded tires.
    • A trophy wall in the cabin where your biggest fish and the legends you land are mounted.
    • A dog that rides in the hot rod and barks when a bear is near.
    • Crab pots at Halibut Pier and from the boat: set them, come back the next day, sell the Dungeness crab.
    • A floatplane trip to a remote lake that no road reaches, for a fee.

sections.title: Hotrod Outdoor Alaska Fishing
sections.html: The game is now called Hotrod Outdoor Alaska Fishing on the title screen, in the page title, in the web app manifest, on the privacy page and as the iPhone app's name under its icon. Saved games keep their old storage names, so a game in progress carries on under the new name.

figs.caption: The title screen with the new name.

sections.title: The dark green line is the perfect throw
sections.html: The timing bar now reads the way you described it. The dark green line in the middle is the perfect throw; light green either side of it is a good cast, orange a weak one and red at the ends a backlash. The white line is the timing marker, sweeping back and forth across the bar (eight passes at most) until you tap. The perfect window is 56 milliseconds wide and the whole green 278 milliseconds, at 0.9 bar widths a second. The line over the water still shows where the lure will land before you let go.

figs.caption: The white marker sweeping toward the dark green line; the dashed line and ring on the water show where the lure will land.

sections.title: A boat with an outboard, on a trailer behind the hot rod
sections.html:
The garage sells a sixteen-foot aluminium skiff with an outboard on a trailer for $1,500. The trailer hitches to the hot rod and follows it round the map, swinging wide on the bends, and you can back it up. Stop near a lake, the river or the bay and tap LAUNCH: the boat slides off the trailer into the water. Walk up to it and tap BOARD, hold GAS and steer as in the car; the camera button switches between the seat at the tiller and a chase view. FISH drops anchor so you can stand and cast all round the boat, and bears cannot reach you out there. ASHORE steps you off where the water meets the land, and LOAD BOAT winches it back onto the trailer. A bigger outboard ($900) takes the top speed from 31 to 49 kilometres an hour.

The boat bobs on the waves of the bay, lifts its bow when it gets up to speed, leans into turns and leaves a wake. The river carries it along, and after the audit it scrapes off the bridge pier, the pier pilings, the docks and the wreck instead of passing through them, and stops at the lip of Bear Falls instead of going over.

figs.caption: The boat on its trailer behind the hot rod.
Running the river in the chase view.
Anchored and casting from the boat.
Full gas at the bridge: the boat scrapes round the middle pier.
Full gas toward the lip of Bear Falls: the boat stops above the drop.

sections.title: Grizzlies and black bears come for your fish, not for you
sections.html:
A bear now only comes for you when there are fish in your cooler or chest freezer. With an empty cooler they leave you alone: they fish at Bear Falls, wander, and move off. With fish aboard, the more you carry the sooner one turns up, and it stalks, bluffs and charges as before.

Black bears now live in the thick forest alongside the grizzlies. They are smaller, swipe lighter, bluff more often and run off when hurt. A bear whistler arrow shrieking past any bear sends it running, which is also the campground ranger's odd job. In the car or out on the boat, no bear can get at you.

sections.title: A small map out of the way, a big map with the fish on it, and RUN
sections.html:
The small map sits in the top left corner, under the money and the cooler and clear of every button. It turns as you do and shows the land, the places you know, the hot rod, the boat, your next goal and a charging bear; it zooms out while you drive, and a tap opens the full map.

The full map now fills the whole screen instead of a small window. Drag it, pinch or use the buttons to zoom. Tap a place, or the lake, river or sea it fishes, to see which fish live there, for example halibut, northern pike and sockeye salmon. Only places you have been to show their fish; the rest say "Explore to find it". Each place also shows the bite there right now and the hours when each fish bites best.

RUN is a button on the left: tap it to run, tap it again to walk. It glows while you run, and hides in the car and the boat.

figs.caption: The small map in the top left, clear of the buttons; RUN on the left.
RUN switched on.
The full map, filling the screen.

sections.title: A wardrobe behind the T-shirt button
sections.html:
A T-shirt button now sits at the top right next to the map, the journal and pause. It opens the wardrobe, with a portrait of Ruben that changes as you pick. Everything shows on your own sleeves and hands in first person and on Ruben at the wheel of the hot rod.

  • Shirts (9): red flannel, blue flannel, forest flannel, denim jacket, black hoodie, camo jacket, hi-vis rain jacket, Hawaiian shirt ($120) and the Hotrod racing jacket ($400).
  • Hats (7): orange cap, trucker cap, wool beanie, bucket hat, cowboy hat, the moose antler hat ($250) and no hat.
  • Beards (5): full beard, lumberjack beard, handlebar mustache, stubble and clean shaven.
  • Hair (5): brown, black, blond, ginger and grey.
  • Skin (5) tones, from pale to dark.
  • Gloves (3): leather gloves, fingerless wool and bare hands.

sections.title: FISH ON! IT THREW THE HOOK! NEW SPECIES!
sections.html:
The big moments are now shouted by an arcade announcer, in the spirit of Sega Bass Fishing, with a banner across the screen to match. The voice is the phone's own speech, pitched down and hyped up, so it adds nothing to the download; it can be switched off in Settings, and the banners still show.

  • Hooked: FISH ON!, FISH ON! FISH ON!, HOOKED UP!, GOT ONE!
  • During the fight: IT'S A BIG ONE!, MONSTER ON THE LINE!, HOLD ON TIGHT!, IT'S JUMPING!, LOOK AT IT GO!, AIRBORNE!
  • Lost: IT THREW THE HOOK!, OH NO, THE HOOK CAME OFF!, OH NO! IT SHOOK THE HOOK!, SNAP! THE LINE BROKE!, OH NO! IT BROKE OFF!, SPOOLED! IT TOOK ALL YOUR LINE!, IT GOT AWAY!, AN EAGLE STOLE IT!
  • Landed: NEW SPECIES! with the name (NEW SPECIES! NORTHERN PIKE!), PERSONAL BEST! with the weight, LEGENDARY! with the legend's name, NICE FISH!, LANDED!, WHAT A CATCH!, BEAUTIFUL!
  • Casting and the hook set: PERFECT CAST!, BIRD'S NEST! (a backlash), TOO EARLY!, TOO SLOW!, MISSED IT!
  • The rest: THE BITE IS ON!, LOOK OUT! (a bear), BULLSEYE! (a head shot with the bow), WHAT A SHOT! and FRAME IT! (a three-star picture), TREASURE!, CHA-CHING! and JOB DONE! (odd jobs), and BIGFOOT?!

sections.title: Fish bite by the weather and the time of day
sections.html:
A BITE readout under the top buttons says how hungry the fish are right now: SLOW, FAIR, GOOD or HOT. Tap it and it says why. The rules follow what anglers know:

  • The dawn bite (from 4:30 to 8:30) is the best of the day, the evening rise (19:00 to 22:30) nearly as good.
  • Under a bright midday sun with a clear sky the fish sulk deep; at night most go quiet, though the burbot prowl the lakes and the dogfish come close in on the sea.
  • A front rolling in (the clouds or the rain building) switches them on; rain on the water and a grey sky make them bolder; a clearing sky behind the rain slows them again.
  • On the sea, the tide matters most: two high tides a day, 12 hours 25 minutes apart, and the fish feed on the moving water either side of slack.
  • Each of the 31 species keeps its own hours on top of that: king salmon at dawn, pike in the midday warmth, burbot at night. The full map shows the best hours for every fish at each place.

The time it takes a fish to bite, and which fish it is, follow the readout.

figs.caption: A HOT bite at dawn with a front coming in.
A tap on the readout says why.

sections.title: Take pictures of fish, moose and bears, and keep them in an album
sections.html:
The Trading Post sells a camera for $250. It joins the rod and the bow on the tool button. Raise it and a viewfinder frames exactly what the picture will keep; the zoom button steps through 1, 2, 4 and 8 times, and the viewfinder names what you are pointing at with up to three stars for how well it fills the frame. A hill, tall grass close in front, a tree's crown or a bush between you and the animal spoils the shot, and an animal partly hidden gets a star less for each hidden part; you can shoot under a birch's leaves, not through a spruce.

Every picture goes into the album in the journal, with a page for each of 65 subjects: 15 land animals, 12 birds, 5 sea mammals, two moments (Old Faceful erupting and Bigfoot) and all 31 fish. The best picture of each is kept, with the time and the place, and the last eight pictures are on a roll. When you land a fish, a camera button on the catch card takes its picture. The magazine Alaska Outdoors buys the first picture of each animal and moment: a three-star shot pays from $10 for a gull to $100 for the orcas, and $300 for Bigfoot; fewer stars pay less. Photographing eight different animals is a challenge worth $400.

sections.title: Steaming Springs, Mosquito Flats and Shipwreck Cove
sections.html:
Each new place has its own landscape, its own fish, a legendary fish, a road to it, a sign at the parking bay and something silly to do.

Steaming Springs

A warm, milky green trout pond in a basin of white and orange sinter, with steam rising off the water, steam vents and bubbling mud pots. Old Faceful, a geyser, rumbles and then blows a column of water and steam every minute or two; its sign says "Stand back. No, further". In the hot pool you can SOAK: an hour passes and every ache goes with it. Rainbow trout, grayling, Dolly Varden, char, whitefish and blackfish live in the warm pond, and the legend is Old Steamy, an 11.4-kilogram rainbow. Nothing lives in the hot pool.

Mosquito Flats

Tea-dark sloughs in the coastal muskeg at the end of Muskeg Road, with a boardwalk over the bog to a dock, dead snags and the World's Largest Mosquito, a statue of Alaska's unofficial state bird ("Please do not feed"). The mosquitoes swarm and have opinions; a machine by the statue sells bug dope for $15, which keeps them off for two hours. Northern pike, sheefish and Alaska blackfish live in the sloughs, and the legend is Sheezilla, a 27-kilogram sheefish.

Shipwreck Cove

The Unsinkable II, a rusty trawler from Homer, has sat aground off the beach since 1987 ("She sank in four feet of water"). Walk the gangplank onto her deck, fish the deep water off her stern for rockfish, lingcod and the wolf eel, open the sea chest in her wheelhouse, and look out at the sea stacks white with birds. The legend is Davy Jones, a 36-kilogram lingcod.

sections.kicker: Adventure, humour and a hairy rumour
sections.title: Odd jobs, Bigfoot, a sea chest and three more legends
sections.html:
Odd jobs. The locals at the Kenai Trading Post always want something. A new Odd jobs tab shows three of them a day; take one at a time, do it, and collect the money back at the Trading Post. Fish jobs hand over the cheapest fish that will do, never a legend while a plain fish is there, and the Collect button names the fish first.

WhoWantsPays
Mrs. HendersonA Northern Pike over 6 kg for her famous pike casserole. Nobody has the heart to tell her.$260
The Kenai GazetteA three-star picture of a bald eagle for Sunday's front page.$200
Dale from the late-night radio showA picture of Bigfoot. Any picture.$1000
The cannery foremanThree Sockeye Salmon before the boss notices.$300
Old EarlHis lucky lure, lost at Salmon Bend in 1974: keep casting there and you might hook it.$240
A tourist from OhioA picture of a moose. "A real one, not the mosquito."$150

A fisheries scientistA Sheefish from Mosquito Flats. She promises it will barely notice.$520
Captain GusA picture of the orcas, to prove the Unsinkable II never sailed alone.$350

The campground rangerA bear moved along without anyone getting hurt: a bear whistler arrow should do it.$300
Your aching backA soak in the hot pool at Steaming Springs. It is not asking.$80
The Bear Falls fish counterA King Salmon over 20 kg, to settle a bet with the bears.$650
The aquarium in SewardA Wolf Eel from Shipwreck Cove. Its face, mostly.$900

Bigfoot. Very rarely, at dawn or dusk, something big and hairy strolls along the edge of the forest a long way off, and lopes away if you get closer than 45 metres. Every picture of it comes out blurry, as tradition demands, and the announcer shouts BIGFOOT?! A picture is worth up to $300 to the magazine and $1,000 to Dale's radio show.

The sea chest in the Unsinkable II's wheelhouse holds $600 in soggy bills, a captain's cap and an IOU for one boat, signed "Gus".

Legends. Three more legendary fish, one at each new place: Old Steamy, Sheezilla and Davy Jones, nine in all.

Challenges. Six more: buy the boat, launch it and land a fish from it; soak in the hot pool; catch a sheefish at Mosquito Flats; walk the gangplank onto the Unsinkable II; land a wolf eel at Shipwreck Cove; and photograph eight different animals.

Humour runs through it: "The mosquitoes have formed a union. They want more Ruben"; the hot pool's sign says "Soak at your own risk · No moose · No boiling your catch"; a moose watches you soak and looks jealous; the Golden Hotrod is "Completely unnecessary. Absolutely essential."; a bear whistler sends a bear running, "So does everyone else within a mile."

sections.title: Gus's paraglider, the key on the ledge and the chest behind the falls
sections.html:
Off every map, Gus (the old-timer whose IOU is in the Unsinkable II's sea chest) left his paraglider on a summit in the far west, 447 m up. You get a glimpse of it from the valley: from Hotrod Landing, where the game starts, the Trading Post, Glacier Lake, Halibut Pier and most other places, a tin mirror on his gear box glints in the sun every few seconds, and after dark a lantern on his windsock pole glows high on the mountain. Nothing of it shows on the map, the small map or the compass, and the README keeps the details in a closed spoiler box.

  1. The climb. About one and a half kilometres on foot from Bear Falls, the upper half steep; four cairns mark the way. At the top: the gear box with the paraglider in a red stuff sack, an orange windsock and a sign, GUS'S LAUNCH · No refunds · Mind the first step. TAKE PARAGLIDER, and the announcer shouts A PARAGLIDER!
  2. The glide. At any edge where the ground 25 m ahead is at least 12 m lower and nothing is in the way, a GLIDE button appears. You run a few steps and the wing lifts you. Drag on the left to steer, up to dive and down to brake; look round with the right. At trim the wing sinks 1.15 m a second at 36 km/h, a glide of about 8.7 to 1; diving is 50 km/h and 2.9 m a second, braking 27 km/h and 0.95. The instruments show your height over the ground, the sink and the speed; your hands hold the brake toggles and pull on the side you turn to; look up and the red and yellow wing is overhead; the wind rises with the speed. You land when your feet touch the ground, a deck or water (in deep water you swim to the nearest shore). A treetop, a roof, a rock or a pole ends the flight early, and a headwind turns you back at the edge of the map.
  3. The ledge. Gus's note points south, to his camp under an orange tarp on a ledge no path reaches, 300 m away and 48 m lower: half a minute in the air. In the grotto: his rolled mat, a pot, a lantern on a post at the mouth (it glows at night, seen from the summit) and a tin with a brass key. TAKE KEY. You can GLIDE on from the ledge.
  4. The chest. The key's note sends you to Bear Falls. From the west bank a stone shelf runs along the foot of the cliff behind the falling water; Gus's chest sits in a niche there, out of sight from the bank. Without the key it is locked tight. OPEN: $5,000 in gold nuggets, TREASURE! GUS'S GOLD!, and Gus's Golden Spoon, a lure every fish takes well and that tilts the odds 40 % toward rare and epic fish. It is never sold at the Trading Post.

Gus's three notes are kept in the journal, under Challenges. A save made in the air keeps the edge you launched from. Bears give up on you when you take off, as they do when you get into the car.

sections.title: Sharper mountains, a new Bear Falls and textures at twice the resolution
sections.html:
The aim was more detail without more work for the phone's graphics processor. Each picture pair below is the same view in the build before this round and in this one.

  • The mountains. The distant terrain is now twice as fine (a point every 20 metres instead of 40) in the 700-metre band round the playable land where the nearest mountains rise: about 128,000 triangles instead of about 61,000, still drawn in one go. Beyond 140 metres, steep slopes also get crags, gullies and buttresses a few tens of metres across in the lighting alone, more than the mesh could carry, and the gullies hold shade and old snow. That costs two texture reads per pixel, and only on far steep slopes.
  • Bear Falls was rebuilt: the river now runs flat to a lip and pours over it in two curved sheets of water, a back sheet and a front sheet that bows out in the middle, split into three falls by boulders on the lip. The water speeds up and turns white as it falls, with ragged edges, a foam pool at the foot, rocks that shine wet and more spray and mist. It is four draws.
  • The new models are built for close looks: the boat's hull is lofted from seven cross sections, with a painted stripe, gunwale rails, three benches, floorboards, a fuel tank, a cooler, a rod in its holder and an outboard with its tiller, skeg and propeller; the trailer has its winch post, carpeted bunks and tail lights. The Unsinkable II's hull is lofted the same way, rust below her old waterline and streaks down her black sides, with a wheelhouse, a mast and rigging, crab pots and a life ring. Ruben now sits at the wheel of the hot rod in your clothes. The earlier rounds rebuilt the trees, the animals and the fish.
  • Textures at twice the resolution: the ground detail (512 texels, was 256), the ripples on the water (512, was 256) and the close-up ground of pebbles, rock beds and needles (1024, was 512), so the ground stays sharp at your feet on a Retina screen. With mipmaps a bigger texture costs the graphics processor about the same to read; the cost is about 6 MB more graphics memory and 0.8 seconds more on the loading screen on the build machine, where the textures are made.

sections.title: Light that follows the hour, and an eye that adapts
sections.html:
The big lighting work was done in the earlier rounds: sun shadows in cascades, mountains that shade the valleys, less sky light in gullies and under the forest, leaves that glow with the sun behind them, cloud shadows, valley mist, wet ground after rain, and bloom and sun rays on the High setting. This round adds four things, none of which costs the graphics processor anything worth measuring:

  • Steam, spray and mist take the light of the hour. Before, every puff of steam, the spray at Bear Falls, splashes, smoke and dust had a fixed colour, so they glowed white in the middle of the night and stayed white at sunset. Now they are lit by the sky and the sun: dark at night like everything else, warm at dawn and dusk. It is worked out once per particle, not per pixel.
  • Steam and spray glow with a low sun behind them, as water droplets do, so the hot pool and Old Faceful light up at dusk.
  • Bear Falls and the geyser fall into shadow. They now darken where a mountain or a cloud shades them, like everything else in the world, instead of shining in full sun in a shaded gorge.
  • The eye adapts. Under the trees, in a cloud's shadow and on a grey day the view opens up by up to 18 % over a second or two, and looking into a low sun it closes down by up to 12 %, the way your eyes and a camera do. Stepping out of the forest into a sunlit meadow, the light is bright for a moment. The night is left as it was.

sections.title: Laid out for every screen size
sections.html:
The top bar was measured at ten screen sizes with the longest goal the game has, from the smallest iPhone to a desktop window, and on the common iPhone also with the notch's safe areas. Three rules keep it clear:

  • The compass and the goal are as wide as the gap between the health bar and the top buttons allows, the notch included; a goal too long for the gap ends in "...". Before, a long goal ran under the health bar and the T-shirt button on the most common iPhone size, 844 by 390 points.
  • On screens narrower than 1,500 points the clock and the bite readout sit under the buttons; in one row with them they overlapped the compass on an iPad.
  • On a phone held upright, or an iPad in a narrow split view, there is no gap: the buttons are smaller, the bite readout sits over the clock, and the compass and the goal move under them, right of the small map. Before, the goal shrank to nothing there, the compass ran over the buttons, the T-shirt button touched the health bar and the bite readout covered the lure.

The map's buttons are smaller on short screens, and the full map always fills the screen: you can no longer drag past the edge of the world into an empty strip.

sections.title: Every bug found, and what was done about it
sections.html:
After the features were in, the whole round was audited. Three separate code reviews each took one part (the camera, the jobs and the screens; the three new places; the boat), and I went through the rest myself and ran every feature in the test browser. A fourth review then checked the fixes themselves, and a fifth everything fixed after that (the signs, the lighting, the top bar and the tree check). The secret had two reviews of its own: a sixth went through all of it, and a seventh checked those fixes and looked again (the rows marked Paraglider, The ledge, The chest, The glimpse and Messages). Altogether 98 problems were found: 67 by the reviews, 12 in my own checks, 4 by the new layout tests and 15 while building and testing. All are fixed. The last column says how each fix was checked: a test means a browser test that drives the game and checks the result, "code review" that the fix was read and reasoned through but not played.

sections.title: What was tested on the final build
sections.html:
Each test is a script in tools/scenarios that drives the game in a browser engine with real taps and checks the result; the numbers below are what the final build reported. They were run one at a time on the build machine's software renderer. All tests passed. The three tests of the secret, boat-falls and eight earlier tests (catch, announcer-bite, ui-check, areas, wardrobe, layout-sizes, bears-arrows and the first half of boat) ran on this round’s build; the other six (timing-bar, camera, jobs-bigfoot, bigfoot-forest, layout-ipad and layout-phone-small) ran on the build before it, and this round changed nothing they use except where messages sit while a banner shows. Some tests needed fixing themselves along the way, none because of the game: the announcer’s banners pop and fade within two seconds, quicker than the software renderer draws a frame, so those tests run with reduced motion and hold each banner; with reduced motion every change of layout is a very short transition that lands a frame or two later, so the screen-size test and the secret’s tests switch transitions off; and Bigfoot strolls on while the slow renderer aims, so the two Bigfoot tests hold him still between the look through the lens and the picture. The Bigfoot forest test also checks the lens against the picture itself: it paints him a flat magenta and counts how many of his pixels the real view shows.

TestWhat it doesWhat the final build did
secretBear Falls from the bank (the chest must not show), the shelf behind the water and the chest without the key, Gus's launch, TAKE PARAGLIDER and his note, and GLIDE at the edge.Passed. From the bank 34 m away the chest did not show; on the shelf (a deck 0.5 m over the pool) OPEN was offered and, without the key, said "Locked tight. A brass keyhole, and a G scratched in the lid"; at the cache, 447 m up, TAKE PARAGLIDER gave A PARAGLIDER! PROPERTY OF GUS with his note below the banner, and the stuff sack left the box; at the edge GLIDE was offered.
secret-flightGLIDE from the summit, three seconds of flight in the game loop, the wing overhead, the rest of the flight to the ledge with an autopilot steering as a player would, the grotto, TAKE KEY, and GLIDE again from the ledge.Passed. After 3.2 seconds in the game loop the pilot was 72 m over the ground at 50 km/h, diving at 2.9 m a second, with the instruments reading the same, the cast button hidden and the hands on the brakes; looking up showed the wing. The rest of the flight, with the same flight code, landed after 26.1 seconds 5.1 m from the key with the wing put away; in the grotto TAKE KEY gave A SECRET KEY! GUS LEFT A NOTE with the note readable below it; on the ledge, facing north, GLIDE was offered again.
secret-treasureThe chest opened with the key, Gus's notes in the journal, the Golden Spoon in the tackle box and not in the shop, the map, and the glint and the lantern seen from Hotrod Landing.Passed. With the key, OPEN gave TREASURE! GUS’S GOLD!, the money went from $150 to $5,250, the gold showed in the open chest and the Golden Spoon joined the tackle box (second in the list, after the free spinner); the journal kept Gus’s three notes; the Trading Post’s tackle tab did not list the spoon; the map showed the twelve places and nothing else. From Hotrod Landing the glint flashed on the summit 1,216 m away and 440 m up, and after dark the lantern there glowed.
areasSteaming Springs with Old Faceful blowing, a soak in the hot pool at 23:30, Bear Falls, the mountains, Mosquito Flats and its boardwalk, Shipwreck Cove from the beach, up the gangplank, round the wheelhouse to the stern, and 60 gold hotspots from the stern.Passed. 9 steam vents and 2 mud pots at Steaming Springs and the geyser blowing; SOAK at 23:30 ended at 0:30 on day 2 with full health and the challenge paid; the mosquitoes swarmed at the Flats; up the gangplank onto the wreck (the deck challenge paid), then round the wheelhouse to the stern in five legs, ending 0.36 m from the fishing spot at deck height 2.66 m; water 3.0 m deep 25 m ahead; 60 of 60 gold hotspots in deep water and none inside the hull; the cast aim found water. Run again on this round’s build: passed the same way, the walk to the stern ending 0.10 m from the fishing spot.
boatBuying the boat, LAUNCH from the trailer, BOARD, four seconds of gas, the chase camera, full gas at the bridge pier and at the lip of Bear Falls, FISH at anchor, LOAD BOAT and the save.Passed. The boat cost $1,500; LAUNCH from the trailer put it in 0.86 m of water; BOARD from the bank 2.3 m away; four seconds of gas reached 7.6 m/s (27 km/h); the chase camera; full gas from 26 m at the bridge pier: the boat came no closer than 3.28 m to its middle and scraped round it; full gas toward Bear Falls: it stopped 1.2 m short of the 13.1 m drop; FISH anchored it with the rod out, DRIVE offered and no bear able to reach you; LOAD BOAT winched it on and the car was towing it at once; the save kept it on the trailer. Run again on this round’s build: passed the same way up to the bridge pier (3.32 m), then the test browser itself gave out at the picture at the falls after about eight minutes, as it now does on the previous round’s build too; the second half passes on its own as boat-falls.
boat-fallsThe second half of the boat test on its own: full gas toward the lip of Bear Falls, FISH at anchor, LOAD BOAT and the save.Passed. Full gas from 30 m above the lip of Bear Falls stopped the boat 2 m short of the 13.1 m drop; FISH anchored it with the rod out and no bear able to reach you; LOAD BOAT winched it onto the trailer, the car towed it at once and the save kept it there.
jobs-bigfootThe odd jobs board, the Bigfoot job, Bigfoot through the 8 times lens, the picture, the reward, the cannery's three sockeye and the album.Passed. The board offered three different jobs (a tourist from Ohio, Chef Rosa and a fisheries scientist); with the Bigfoot job taken, from a meadow by the forest at dusk, Bigfoot stepped out 95 m away with no hill, grass, tree or bush between; through the 8 times lens he filled 30 % of the picture for three stars; the picture went into the album, the job was done and paid $1,000; the cannery’s job was not ready with two sockeye and ready with three, and it took the sockeye and left the pink salmon in the cooler.
bigfoot-forestBigfoot from three spots deep in the forest at dusk, through the 8 times lens: does he step out only where you can see him?Passed. At dusk, from two of the three spots deep in the forest Bigfoot stepped out, 101 m and 125 m away, and the lens gave three stars with all three sight lines clear; painted a flat magenta and counted, 97 % and 62 % of his pixels showed in the frame. From the third spot, with 46 spruce within 30 m, he found no clear spot and did not appear.
ui-checkThe title, the small map clear of the buttons, RUN on and off, the full map filling the screen, a tap on Moose Lake, on the river and on Salmon Bend, and the fit button.Passed. The small map (80 by 80 points at the top left) does not overlap RUN; RUN lit on the first tap and went out on the second; the full map filled 820 by 370 points of the 844 by 390 screen; Moose Lake showed its six fish with their best hours and the bite there; a tap on the river picked Salmon Bend, 70 m away; the fit button showed the whole map. Run again on this round’s build: passed the same way.
timing-barThe power needle and the ring over the water, the timing marker on the dark green line (a perfect cast into the ring), the orange (hooked left) and the red (a backlash).Passed. The ring sat where a cast at that power lands (11.8 m at 30 % power, 19.6 m at 60 %), gold over the hotspot; the white marker swept the timing bar; a tap on the dark green line made a perfect cast that landed 0.00 m from the centre of the ring; a tap in the red at the left end was a backlash. The throw line costs 6 draws and 620 triangles.
bears-arrowsBears with an empty cooler and with a fish in it, black bears, selling the fish mid-charge, the arrow shop, the arrows chip and a bear whistler past a charging bear.Passed. 7 grizzlies and 3 black bears. With an empty cooler a roaming grizzly kept roaming and a stalking one backed off; with one sockeye in the cooler it went alert, charged and attacked; selling the fish mid-alert sent it away. A black bear did the same, and fled after an arrow. All five arrow kinds were on sale; whistlers stopped at 12; a tap on the chip nocked a whistler, and one loosed past a charging bear sent it running. The 7 arrows in a save from before became 7 cedar arrows. Run again on this round’s build: passed the same way.
announcer-biteThe bite readout at midday and at dawn with a front and rain, a tap on it, the FISH ON!, NEW SPECIES!, long name and hook-off banners, and the bite on the map.Passed. At midday in sunshine the readout said SLOW; at dawn with a front and rain it said HOT, glowed, and the announcer called THE BITE IS ON!; a tap on it explained: Dawn bite, A front is rolling in, Rain on the water. The banners FISH ON!, NEW SPECIES! NORTHERN PIKE!, a long species name and OH NO, THE HOOK CAME OFF! all showed, and are in the pictures. Halibut Pier on the map listed its 16 fish with their best times (running tide, dawn, night, rain) and the bite there. Run again on this round’s build: passed the same way.
wardrobeThe T-shirt button and the top bar, buying and wearing clothes, not enough money, the sleeves and gloves in first person, Ruben at the wheel and the save.Passed. The T-shirt button sits with the map, journal and pause buttons, the bite readout and clock under them; the wardrobe offered 34 options; the Hawaiian shirt cost $120; the antler hat was refused with $30 left and bought after; the whole look (shirt, brown skin, antler hat, handlebar mustache, ginger hair, fingerless wool gloves) showed on the portrait, on 96 of the 396 sleeve vertices in first person and on Ruben at the wheel, and survived a save. Run again on this round’s build: passed the same way.
cameraBuying the camera, the viewfinder on a moose at 4 and 1 times, a three-star picture and its sale, the catch card's camera button and the album.Passed. The camera cost $250; at 4 times the viewfinder named the moose 30 m away, with three stars once the lens had zoomed in; the picture went into the album with three stars and Alaska Outdoors paid $40 for it; the catch card’s camera button took a three-star picture of a sockeye and then greyed out; the album showed 65 pages, two with pictures; the stored album took 21 KB.
catchA whole catch with real taps: cast, bite, hook, fight and land, then the journal, the map, the shop and the tackle tab.Passed. CAST, power set at 60 %, the timing tap, the flight and the landing; a bite, HOOK and the fight; the catch card showed a Dolly Varden; KEEP put it in the cooler and the first challenge paid $50; the journal, the map, the shop and the tackle tab opened. Run again on this round’s build: passed the same way, with a steelhead this time.
layout-ipadThe title, the top bar, the map, the wardrobe and the jobs on an iPad-sized screen (1180 by 820).Passed. On the 1180 by 820 screen no two controls on the playing screen overlapped, also with the longest goal, which fits on one line (603 points wide); the map filled the screen; the wardrobe showed all 34 options without scrolling, and the jobs board its three jobs side by side.
layout-phone-smallThe same on a small phone (667 by 375).Passed. On the 667 by 375 screen no two controls on the playing screen overlapped, also with the longest goal: the compass (253 points) and the goal (259 points, ending in "...") keep to the gap between the health bar and the top buttons; the map, the wardrobe and the jobs board open as scrolling sheets.
layout-sizesThe top bar with the longest goal at ten screen sizes: the common iPhone sideways (844 by 390), with and without the notch's safe areas; the largest and the smallest iPhone sideways; an iPhone held upright; an iPad Air upright, sideways and in a narrow split view; a 12.9-inch iPad Pro sideways; and desktop windows 1,500 and 1,920 wide.Passed. At all ten sizes, and on the common iPhone also with the notch's 59-point safe areas, no two controls on the playing screen overlapped with the longest goal showing. The goal fits on one line on the iPads sideways and 1,920 points wide (603 points) and ends in "..." elsewhere, from 230 points on a phone held upright to 560 at 1,500 wide; with the notch the compass and the goal narrow to 318 points between the health bar and the buttons; on the phone held upright and in the narrow split view they sit under the top rows. Run again on this round’s build: passed the same way.

Some fixes are about the world's shape and the colliders, which are quicker and more thorough to check in node with the game's own code than by playing:

CheckResult
The trout pond at Steaming Springs and Big SloughBoth hold water again: 3,944 m² up to 5.3 m deep, and 6,344 m². 45 of 45 points in front of each new fishing spot are water.
Casting from Shipwreck CoveFrom the old spot on the beach, 57 % of cast lines crossed the hull. From the stern, every point a cast can reach is water, deep enough for gold hotspots.
The walk to the sternFrom the beach up the gangplank and round either side of the wheelhouse to the fishing spot, also when weaving; walking into the crab pots is blocked; the hatch is a 0.44 m step up.
Rocks under the boat and on landOnly the 118 rocks under water have a height the boat can pass over. 112 of them lie below the keel in water deep enough for the boat, and the boat passes over all of them; the 11 that reach up to the keel still stop it. All 4,611 rocks on land stop someone walking and the hot rod coming at them from their uphill side.
A boat beyond the marginA save with the boat 8 m from the map edge loads with the boat on its trailer. A boat out there drives back inside the margin within 10 seconds; heading out to sea, it stops 30 m inside the edge.
The bridge pierThe fourth review drove the boat at the pier from every side offset between 6 m left and 6 m right: it never passed through.
Bigfoot in sightWith the real trees, willows, bushes, fireweed, ferns and grass, checked along three lines to him: from 12 meadows by the forest he stepped out at 11 (45 looks in all); at the twelfth you stand in a willow's leaves, where no look is clear. From 12 spots deep in the forest he stepped out at 11 (107 looks); the twelfth is thick spruce. Where he finds no clear spot, the game tries again 20 seconds later.
Bushes and flowers in the wayOf 480 random sight lines 40 to 140 m long from a standing eye to something 1.2 m tall, bushes, fireweed or ferns block 22 % from a meadow by the forest and 29 % in deep forest (tree crowns 51 % and 80 %). One check takes about 4 microseconds.
The far terrain at the map edgeNo cell of the far terrain or of its coarse copy for the reflection overlaps the playable ground. The copy's heights match a fresh calculation exactly, and it is made in half the time.
The sharper texturesMade in 1.1 seconds instead of 0.3 on the build machine.
Gus’s launchFacing the ledge, GLIDE is offered at 21 spots and headings round the cache. From four of them an autopilot that steers as a player would lands 2.9 to 3.0 m from the ledge after 25.5 to 26.2 seconds.
A pilot who only holds a headingLaunched 176 to 184 degrees and never steering, with or without diving near the end, the pilot passes the ledge 12 to 16 m up and comes down on the slope behind it, 8 to 31 m away. From all six landings tried, walking round the front of the grotto reaches 1.2 m from the key (2.1 m is enough).
The ledgeNo path reaches it (the second review checked with a walk in 5 cm steps at just under the walking slope limit). GLIDE is offered from it at 55 of the spots and headings tried.
The chestFrom the west bank onto the shelf (a 0.5 m step up) and along it to 1.9 m from the chest (2.4 m is enough), never in water deeper than the shelf allows.
The glimpseLines of sight from a standing eye: the glint and the summit lantern can be seen from all 49 spots tried at Hotrod Landing, the Trading Post, Glacier Lake and Kachemak Light, 47 at Halibut Pier, 44 to 48 at Steaming Springs, 41 at Caribou Tundra, 37 at Mosquito Flats and 27 to 28 at Bear Falls; not from Salmon Bend, Moose Lake or Shipwreck Cove. The grotto’s lantern shows from 14 of 24 spots round the summit cache.
Edge cases in the airAt the edge of the map a headwind turns the glider back 1,153 to 1,161 m from the middle (the limit is 1,170). Into a spruce crown: "You snag a treetop", down 1.0 m from its trunk. Into a 13.6 by 9.6 m building 3 m up: "Bonk!", down beside it. Into Halibut Pier’s side walls from either side: standing in 0.5 m of water. Round Bear Falls GLIDE is offered at 922 spots and headings, and 1 of those launches splashes down within 2 seconds.

sections.title: What all this costs the phone
sections.html:
The same eight views as in the earlier rounds, on the High setting, in the build before this round and in this one, plus the three new places. Draw calls and triangles are counted exactly for each frame, but animals, birds and particles move between runs, so the same view varies by up to about 3 % in triangles and a dozen draws from one run to the next; the software renderer's frame times say nothing about a phone and are left out.

Across the eight views the draws went from 1,739 to 1,656 (-5 %) and the triangles from 7,802,594 to 8,324,920 (+7 %).

  • The mountains account for most of the extra triangles: the finer band of far terrain is 128,000 triangles instead of 61,488, in the one draw that was there before. The water's reflection, which redraws the surroundings a face at a time every frame, at first got the fine copy too; it now keeps its own coarse copy, since its 128 to 256 pixel faces cannot show the detail. The views already held about 980,000 triangles on average. The crags and gullies are two texture reads per pixel, on far steep slopes only.
  • Bear Falls is four draws and about 3,000 triangles.
  • The loading screen is about one second longer on the build machine: the sharper textures take 1.1 seconds to make instead of 0.3 and about 6 MB more graphics memory (reading them costs the same as before), and the reflection's coarse copy of the mountains, which takes its heights from the fine one, about a tenth of a second more.
  • The new lighting costs nothing measurable: the particles' light is worked out once per particle, the falls and the geyser read the shadow maps every material already reads, and the eye adaptation is one number for the tone mapping, set on the main processor from a count of nearby trees four times a second.
  • The boat, Bigfoot and the camera draw only when they are there: the boat, the trailer and its two wheels are four draws, Bigfoot five while he walks, and the camera adds nothing until you take a picture, when it copies one frame into a small picture.
  • The announcer uses the phone's own speech, so it adds nothing to the download.

sections.title: What would change this conclusion
sections.html:
The conclusion is that everything on your list is done and the audit's bugs are fixed. These would change it:

  • A real iPhone falling below 60 frames a second at the new places. All measurements here come from a software renderer on the build machine, which counts draws and triangles exactly but says little about a phone's graphics processor. The heaviest new sights are the steam at Steaming Springs and Old Faceful blowing (both share the particle budget the game already had) and the mountains' doubled triangles. If a phone struggles there, the first levers are the far terrain band back to 40 metres on the Medium and Low settings and fewer steam puffs.
  • The announcer's voice on your phone. It uses the phone's own speech voices, pitched down and sped up, so how it sounds depends on the voices installed. If it sounds flat or robotic, the fix is a set of recorded lines, which would add to the download.
  • How the boat handles under a thumb. The steering, the speed and the scrape against piers were tuned with test input in a desktop browser engine. Each is one number.
  • The eye adaptation and the lit steam on a phone screen outdoors. Both were judged on a desktop monitor. The adaptation's range (up to 18 % brighter, 12 % darker) and the steam's glow are each one number.
  • What a picture counts as hidden. The camera's stars take account of hills, the grass, tree crowns, willows, bushes, fireweed and ferns with the sizes and shapes the game draws, along three lines to the animal, but not fallen logs, rocks or the small flowers. In the browser, where the lens said three stars for Bigfoot, 56 to 100 % of him showed, so a picture can be rated a little generously when an animal is a third hidden. If that bothers you on the phone, more lines can be checked.
  • The game's balance. The prices of the rods, arrows, boat and camera, the jobs' rewards, how often a bear comes for your fish and how rarely Bigfoot shows up were set by reasoning, not by playing for hours. If Bigfoot never shows for you, it can be made less shy.
  • The loading screen. The sharper textures and the reflection's copy of the mountains add about one second on the build machine. If it feels long on an older phone, the big ground texture can be made in the background after the game starts.
  • The iPhone app. It carries its own copy of the game and has not been built again; until it is, it does not have this round.
  • How hard the secret is. The climb (about 1.5 km) and the glide (about 300 m with 48 m to lose on an 8.7 to 1 wing) were tuned with simulations and an autopilot, not with a thumb on a phone. If the ledge is too hard to land on, the glide can be made longer or the ledge wider; if the climb is too long, more cairns or a gentler way up.
  • Whether anyone notices the glimpse. The glint flashes every 2.7 seconds for about a quarter of a second, only in sunshine, and the lantern glows only at night. If it goes unnoticed, the flash can come more often or last longer.

footer: Built on the claude/ruben-hotrod-fishing branch: the code on GitHub, the README and the playable build. The game runs on three.js (documentation). Background reading: Sega Bass Fishing for the announcer, geysers, mud pots and sinter for Steaming Springs, muskeg for Mosquito Flats, weather fronts and tides for the bite, mipmaps for why bigger textures cost little to draw, and the eye's adaptation to light. The fish follow what lives in south-central Alaska: sheefish, Alaska blackfish, wolf eel, lingcod and northern pike; and for the secret, paragliding, the glide ratio and cairns. The build machine's network policy blocks these sites, so the links were written from knowledge and not opened from there. Prices in the game are the game's own dollars.
